title: Lakshmi and the Lights
audience: Families and festival audiences; a one-minute Diwali explainer about why Lakshmi is welcomed with light.
tone: warm, clear, devotional without being preachy; a story told by a friend who knows the sources
logline: On the darkest night of Kartik, a row of lamps welcomes Lakshmi, the goddess of prosperity, whose story begins in the churning of the cosmic ocean.

spine.want: to understand why Lakshmi is prayed to on Diwali
spine.obstacle: the festival is many traditions at once, and the story is often told as a list of names
spine.turn: Lakshmi's own story is about prosperity that returns through effort, virtue and generosity
spine.button: light a lamp, make room, share what you have

narration.text: On the darkest night of Kartik, India lights a row of lamps. This is Diwali, the festival of lights.
Why Lakshmi? She is the goddess of prosperity and abundance. Her lotus rises from muddy water and still opens clean.
One beloved story begins in the churning of the cosmic ocean, when gods and asuras sought the nectar of immortality.
Many treasures rose. Then Lakshmi appeared on a lotus, radiant, lotuses in her hands.
She chose Vishnu. Some call Diwali her birthday; others, her wedding.
So homes are cleaned, rangoli drawn at the door, windows left open, diyas lit, a path for her.
Lakshmi Puja asks for prosperity. The old stories add a condition: wealth stays where there is effort, virtue and generosity.
In Bengal the same night is Kali's; in the north, Rama's return; in the west, new account books open.
Light a lamp. Make room. Share what you have. That is how the light comes in, and stays.
